I’m sorry—I don’t have the ability to make outbound HTTP requests from here, so I can’t pull the current weather data directly for you. Below is a quick‑start guide showing **how** you can retrieve exactly what you asked for (hourly temperature, wind speed, and precipitation probability) for the coordinates (37.8651 N, –119.5383 W) over the next ten days using one of the most popular free/open‑weather APIs: **Open Meteo**. --- ## 1️⃣ What You Need | Item | Why | |------|-----| | `Python` ≥ 3.8 | To run the short script below. | | `requests` package | Simple HTTP client (`pip install requests`). | | Internet connection | Needed to hit the API endpoint. | > *If you prefer another language (JavaScript, Go, Bash …) let me know—I'll adapt the example.* --- ## 2️⃣ Quick Test URL (no coding) ``` curl \ "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast\ ?latitude=37.8651\ &longitude=-119.5383\ &hourly=temperature_2m,windspeed_10m,precipitation_probability\ &timeformat=unixtime\ &timezone=America%2FLos_Angeles" ``` This will return a JSON payload containing all available hours (up to ~7 days depending on your plan). For more than seven days you’ll need to request the “daily” series and then interpolate if needed—or switch to a paid tier / other provider. --- ## 3️⃣ Full Example Script (Python) ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ Fetches hourly temperature, windspeed, and precipitation probability for the next 10 days at latitude 37.8651°N, longitude -119.5383°W using the Open-Meteo API. """ import json from datetime import datetime, timedelta import sys try: import requests except ImportError as exc: print("Missing dependency: pip install requests", file=sys.stderr) raise exc def build_url(lat: float, lon: float): """Constructs the query string.""" base = "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast" params = { # Coordinates "latitude": lat, "longitude": lon, # Variables requested per hour "hourly": "temperature_2m,windspeed_10m,precipitation_probability", # Time format (Unix epoch seconds → easier post‑processing) "timeformat": "unixtime", "timezone": "America/Los_Angeles", # local time zone # Optional: limit output to 240 hours (~10 days) "past_days": 0, "future_hours": 240, } # Build full URL manually because requests.get() handles encoding automatically qs = "&".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in params.items()) return f"{base}?{qs}" def main(): LATITUDE = 37.8651 LONGITUDE = -119.5383 url = build_url(LATITUDE, LONGITUDE) print(f"[INFO] Requesting {url}") resp = requests.get(url, timeout=10) resp.raise_for_status() data = resp.json() # Pretty‑print the raw JSON print(json.dumps(data, indent=2)) # Optionally transform into a pandas DataFrame try: import pandas as pd df = ( pd.DataFrame( dict(zip(["datetime"] + list(data["hourly"].keys())[1:], zip(*data["hourly"].values()))) ) .assign(datetime=lambda x: pd.to_datetime(x.datetime, unit="s")) .set_index("datetime") ) print("\n[DATAFRAME HEAD]") print(df.head()) except Exception as exc: print("[WARN] Pandas not installed – skipping dataframe conversion.", file=sys.stderr) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` ### How It Works 1. **URL Construction** – Builds a single GET request specifying: * Latitude & Longitude * Hourly variables (`temperature_2m`, `windspeed_10m`, `precipitation_probability`) * Unix timestamps for easy parsing * Local timezone (“America/Los_Angeles”) so times line up with daylight savings changes * A hard‑coded maximum of 240 future hours (≈ 10 days); adjust if you need fewer/more. 2. **Request & Error Handling** – Uses `requests.get()` with a 10‑second timeout and raises an exception on non‑200 status codes. 3. **Output** – Prints the raw JSON and optionally converts it to a tidy `pandas.DataFrame`. --- ## 4️⃣ Things to Keep in Mind | Topic | Detail | |-------|--------| | **Free Tier Limits** | Open‑Meteo’s free tier caps at 100 000 requests/month and typically provides up to 7 days of hourly data. If you truly need 10 days of hourly resolution, consider upgrading or combining the daily series with interpolation. | | **Units** | Temperature in °C, windspeed in km/h, precipitation probability in %. Convert if you need Fahrenheit/kph/etc. | | **Time Zone** | Setting `"timezone"` ensures returned timestamps match Pacific Daylight/Summer Time where those coordinates lie. | | **Rate Limiting** | Respect the API’s rate limits (usually 60 req/min). Add exponential backoff if you’re looping through many locations. | | **Alternative Providers** | • [Met.no](https://www.met.no/) (Norwegian Meteorological Institute)
• [NOAA Climate Prediction Center](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/)
• Commercial options: AccuWeather, Visual Crossing, Tomorrow.io, Weatherbit, etc. Many offer similar endpoints but might charge after a certain quota. | --- ## 5️⃣ Next Steps * Run the script locally to confirm you receive the expected fields. * Store the resulting CSV/JSON for downstream processing. * If you’d rather see a visual dashboard, pipe the DataFrame into Matplotlib/Plotly or export to Google Sheets. Let me know which part you'd like help expanding—e.g., automating across multiple sites, adding alerts when precipitation > X%, or converting units!
